title: Vamshivadana Thakura
html:
Krishna's Flute

Among the companions of Sri Chaitanya who stayed on in Navadvipa after His sannyasa there is a devotee whose very name tells who he was in Krishna's pastimes. Vaishnavas know him by five names: Vamshivadana (“the one with the flute at his lips” — a name of Krishna too), Vamshidasa, Vamshi, Vadana and Vadananda; the biographies call him Sri Vamshivadanananda Thakura. In the primary sources he is “Vamshidasa Thakkura” in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika,” “Sri Vamshivadana” and “Sri Thakura Vamshi” in the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” “Vamshivadana Dasa” in the “Prema-vilasa,” “Sri Vamshivadana” in the “Narottama-vilasa,” and “Vamshivadana Thakura” and “Vamshivadana Dasa” in the “Vaishnava-vandanas”; his own songs he signed “Vamshi” and “Vamshivadana.” Here we call him Vamshivadana Thakura, or simply Vamshi.1

Kavi Karnapura in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” reveals his place in the eternal lila:

“The flute, dear to Krishna, is Vamshi Dasa Thakura.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika,” 179)

Sri Krishna's flute is no wooden object but His eternal companion, full of consciousness and love (chinmaya), as everything in Vraja is. She alone drinks without cease the nectar of His lips, and the gopis, Krishna's beloved, sang of her good fortune — yet there is no worldly jealousy in their words: it is the voice of their prema, which longs only to serve Krishna as closely as the flute serves Him. That is why the biographies say that the flute of Vraja, wholly spiritual, which touched the nectar of His lips, appeared in Gauranga's lila in the form of Sri Vamshivadana. This is not an object turned into a man but the descent of an eternal associate: the one who sounds on Krishna's lips in Vraja came to Navadvipa as a devotee and servant of the Lord's family.2

The “Vaishnava-vandanas” remember the same. Sri Jiva in the Sanskrit “Vandana” praises “Krishna's flute — Vamshivadana Thakura” (v. 120); the “second” Vrindavana Dasa sings: “I shall praise the feet of Thakura Vamshivadana, who formerly was the flute at Krishna's lips” (v. 112); the “Sri Vaishnavabhidhana” calls him “Sri Vamshivadana Dasa, who revealed the song of the flute” (v. 32); and Devakinandana says, enigmatically: “Gadadhara Dasa made [him] a descent of the flute” (v. 86).3 And Narahari Chakravarti, opening the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” praises him too among the Lord's companions: “Glory to Abhirama, Vamshi, Saranga and Sundara!” (1.29).

Krishnadasa Kaviraja in the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” does not name him; he tells only of the house of Madhava Dasa in Kuliya, where the Lord stayed for a week — the house of his father. Of Vamshi himself we learn from the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika,” the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” the “Prema-vilasa,” the “Narottama-vilasa,” the “Vaishnava-vandanas,” his own songs and family traditions.

The Chattopadhyayas of Kuliya

Vamshi was born in Kuliya — on the far bank of the Ganga, opposite old Navadvipa, in Koladvipa, where the town of Navadvipa stands today. Kuliya consisted of four quarters — Teghari, Benchi, Yara-Bedrapara and Chinedanga.4 According to the “Shripata-paryatana,” Kuliya and neighbouring Paharpur were two villages where Vamshivadana, Kavidatta and Saranga Thakura lived; when the villages grew and merged, the town came to be called Kulia-Paharpur.

He was a brahmana of the Chattopadhyaya family. Its founder is held to be the renowned Srikara Chattopadhyaya, who, by tradition, came from Bilvagrama and settled in Benchiara, one of the quarters of Kuliya; among his descendants was Yudhishthira Chattopadhyaya.5 Yudhishthira had three sons, and all three bore playful nicknames counted in cowries — the small shells that served as petty coin: the eldest, Madhava Dasa, was Chhakari (“Six Cowries”), the second, Haridasa, Tinkari (“Three Cowries”), and the youngest, Krishna-sampatti, Dukari (“Two Cowries”).6 Vamshi's father was Chhakari — Madhava Dasa Chattopadhyaya, and his mother, Sri Chandrakala Devi.

He appeared on Madhu-purnima, Chaitra's full-moon day — according to some, in 1416 Shaka (1494), according to others, in 1427 Shaka (1505).7 A family work, the “Vamshi-shiksha,” says that on that day, Madhu-purnima of 1416 Shaka, the whole world sings of the festival of Vamshi's appearance. Our calendar, the calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math, marks “the Appearance Day of Srila Vamshivadananda Thakura” on the Purnima at the end of the month of Vishnu, at Vasanta-rasa; in 2026 it fell on 2 April.

Tradition holds that at his birth Sriman Mahaprabhu and Advaita Acharya Prabhu were there. This is a tradition, and the primary sources are silent about it; one biography links it with the days when the Lord stayed in Madhava Dasa's house, but the years do not allow it.8

The Lord's Week in Madhava Dasa's House

Chhakari was devoted to Mahaprabhu with all his heart, and the Lord dearly loved his son Vamshi.

Madhava Dasa's house entered the story of the Lord's pastimes. Five years after His sannyasa Mahaprabhu set out from Puri for Bengal, wishing to see the Ganga and His mother, and visited Navadvipa. Krishnadasa Kaviraja relates:

“Then the Lord stayed in Vachaspati's house, and for fear of the crowds He went on to Kuliya. In Kuliya the son of Shachi lodged in the house of Madhava Dasa, and countless millions of people had His darshana. He stayed there seven days and delivered the people; in His own way He saved even all the offenders.” (CC, Madhya 16.207–209)

Kavi Karnapura in the ninth act of the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” says that the Lord, after visiting Advaita's house, crossed by boat to the far bank opposite Navadvipa, to the village of Kuliya, “to the house of Madhava Dasa,” and out of mercy for Navadvipa's people stayed there seven days. People thronged in such crowds that

“the fence of the strongest, thickest bamboos that Madhava put up at night, the press of the crowds by morning gradually ground to dust” (“Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” 9.16).

The biographies add that in those days, in Chhakari's house, the Lord showed mercy to Navadvipa's residents, forgave all who had once offended Him, and instructed and delivered Devananda Pandita; according to one of them, this was when the Lord went by way of Kuliya on His tour of Bengal that ended at Kanai-natashala.9

Guardian of Shachi and Vishnupriya

When Mahaprabhu took sannyasa and settled in Puri, Vamshivadana was entrusted with the service of guardian and servant (rakshaka-sevaka) of the Lord's mother, Shachi, and of His consort, Vishnupriya Devi. Together with him Ishana Thakura, the old servant in the Lord's house, was blessed with this service.10 To serve the Lord's mother and consort in the days when He had left them for sannyasa is a special fortune, and the biographies speak of it in just those terms: both were “blessed” with this care. In serving them Vamshi served the Lord Himself, for service to those dear to Him is dearer to the Lord than service to Himself.

The grief of Navadvipa after the Lord left for sannyasa Vamshi poured out in a song — the most famous of his padas. In it sounds the separation of Shachi and Vishnupriya, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, and of the poet himself, who was with them:

“No more shall I see on the broad brow the adornment of curls and tilaka, no more see on the golden lotus [of His face] the dance of the wagtail eyes.

No more will He dance in Srivasa's house with His chataka-bird devotees, no more will He dance in His own house for us to gaze at Him.

Will the two brothers, Nimai and Nitai, ever dance together again? I keep crying, ‘Nimai!’ — but Nimai is nowhere.

Pitiless Keshava Bharati came and brought down a thunderbolt on our heads. How, not seeing beautiful Gauranga, shall I stay on in Nadia?

Who is there now to bring back my Gaura Raya? Hearing the weeping of mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, Vamshi rolls in the dust.” (“Pada-kalpataru” 1855)

“Pitiless” here is no reviling of Keshava Bharati, the Lord's sannyasa-guru, through whom the Lord Himself chose to manifest sannyasa, but the reproach of loving hearts from whom separation has taken Gaura. For the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” calls Bharati “a pure soul” (Madhya 28.10) and tells how the Lord Himself, choosing a pretext, whispered the mantra into his ear, mercifully making him His disciple, and only then, at His bidding, did Bharati speak that mantra to the Lord (Madhya 28.154–159): the sannyasa was His own will. This is no worldly despair but the vipralambha of eternal associates, for whom the Lord, hidden from their eyes, becomes all the nearer to the heart. The song shows that Vamshi lived close to Shachi and Vishnupriya then and heard their weeping.11

When Mahaprabhu had withdrawn from sight and Shachimata had left this world, Vamshivadana remained in the Lord's house and served Vishnupriya Devi and Ishana Thakura. He was a disciple (shishya) of Vishnupriya and lived in Mayapur to serve her; he was renowned as her “exclusive vessel of mercy” (ekanta kripa-patra). One biography says that after Mahaprabhu's withdrawal Vishnupriya took him as her servant and that he, as is told, became the first to receive her mercy.12

The Meeting with Srinivasa

The fullest account of Vamshi is preserved in the “Bhakti-ratnakara.” The young Srinivasa, the future acharya, came to Navadvipa to see Vishnupriya's feet, found the Lord's house and stood stock-still before it, looking about him like a wooden doll. Then Vamshi saw him:

“Sri Vamshivadana, seeing him, without any introduction thought to himself, ‘This must be Srinivasa.’ Coming near, he asked who he was; Srinivasa told him everything from beginning to end. Sri Vamshivadana embraced him and bathed Srinivasa in his own tears. Srinivasa, falling to the ground, wishes to bow down, but Sri Thakura Vamshi will not release him from his embrace. To inform Sri Ishvari, Mother Vishnupriya, Sri Vamshivadana went [to her] with care.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara,” 4.20–24)

Vamshi recognised Srinivasa though he had never seen him, and would not let him bow down — so does an eternal associate greet one whom the Lord has already called His own. According to one biography, he blessed the youth, set him on his lap and bathed his head with tears of love; through him Srinivasa was blessed with the darshana of Vishnupriya's feet as well.13

And Vishnupriya at that very time was telling her maidservant of her dream: the Lord had come to her and told her to show mercy to a young brahmana, Srinivasa, who would come that day. And then Vamshi announced:

“‘Srinivasa has come here from Nilachala.’ Hearing this, Ishvari wished to see him.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara,” 4.39–40)

The biographies tell of this meeting in different ways. According to one, Srinivasa found Vamshivadana in Mahaprabhu's house and bowed at his feet; learning who stood before him, Vamshi was overjoyed, loudly called out the name of Sri Chaitanya and asked Vishnupriya to grant the youth her darshana. At first she would not agree; only when Vamshi told her how ardently Srinivasa longed for it, and begged her again and again, did she relent, and at her bidding Vamshi brought him in. According to another, Vamshivadananda, seeing how Srinivasa was languishing in separation from Mahaprabhu, went to Vishnupriya of his own accord and asked her to receive and bless him.

The meeting is recalled with reference to the “Prema-vilasa” as well: when Srinivasa came to Navadvipa for the darshana of Vishnupriya's feet, in Sri Mayapur he met her disciple Vamshivadana Dasa and received the blessing both of Vishnupriya and of her disciple. In the “Prema-vilasa” Srinivasa, having come from Shrikhanda, in separation from Gadadhara Pandita went for days at a time without food, and on the eighth day, utterly wasted, “met Vamshivadana Dasa” (4.169), who asked him who he was and where he came from; but further on, in that book, it is Ishana who looks after the youth.14

Service of the Deities

Vamshi served the Lord not only in those dear to Him but in His Deities as well. From of old Sri Gopinatha, the Deity of his forefathers, had resided in his family, and Vamshi worshipped Him. He himself served Sri Pranavallabha.15 Later on, at Vishnupriya Devi's wish, he instituted the worship of the Deity of Sri Gauranga. This Deity is the Lord Himself, for the Lord's name, Deity and svarupa are one; in serving Pranavallabha, Gopinatha and Gauranga, Vamshi served the Lord Himself.16

After Vishnupriya Devi left this world, the service of the Deities was moved to Kuliya (Kulia-Paharpur).17 And when Vamshi's descendants, taking shelter of the mercy of Sri Jahnava Mata, settled at the shripata of Baghnapara, the service of the Deities in Kuliya was in the hands of servitors (sevaits) from Malhana.

Family

Vamshi lived as a householder; the biographies call this his grihastha-lila — the pastime of an eternal associate in the role of a householder, not worldly family life. He had two sons — Sri Nityananda Dasa (also called Nitai Dasa) and Sri Chaitanya Dasa.

Of Chaitanya Dasa the “Narottama-vilasa” tells. When Sri Jahnava, on her way to the great festival at Kheturi, was at Ambika, he came there with his people:

“Sri Vamshivadana's son Sri Chaitanya Dasa at that moment came with his people to Prabhu. Seeing the feet of Sri Jahnava Ishvari, he deemed himself blessed; streams flowed from both his eyes.” (“Narottama-vilasa,” 6.221–222)

And at Kheturi, at the festival meal, “Sri Vamshivadana's son Sri Chaitanya Dasa ate with his people, rejoicing” (“Narottama-vilasa,” 8.59).

Songs

Vamshivadana was a renowned padakarta, a composer of Vaishnava songs. His songs have a rare sweetness and gentleness and are full of deep devotional feeling. He sang much of Krishna's pastimes: of the dana-lila, when Krishna levies a “toll” on the gopis, of the nauka-vilasa, the pastimes on the boat, and of the vana-vihara, the rambles in the forest.

He sang too of Gauranga's pastimes in Navadvipa. In one of his padas Gora, the son of Shachi, remembering how He herded the cows, calls them by name; Nityananda sounds a call with His mouth, imitating a horn, Gauridasa and Abhirama come running, and Gauranga appears in the dress of Natavara — and the poet concludes: “Says Vamshivadana: ‘Come, let us go to Govardhana!’” (“Pada-kalpataru” 2564). Another pada sings of the eve of a kirtana festival in Advaita's house: Advaita prepares the consecration of the mridanga, Nitai hands out garlands and sandal, Govinda plays the mridanga, Haridasa sings, Srivasa holds the tune, Gora dances — “says Vamshi: ‘Cry out “Glory!”’” (“Pada-kalpataru” 26). Padas signed “Vamshidasa” may not be his at all: that signature was used also by a later poet, a disciple of Srinivasa Acharya.18

Yet the most famous remains the song of separation after the Lord's sannyasa, given above: in it, the biographies say, he expressed the grief of Mother Shachi — and in it his own sorrow can be heard as well.

Last Years

At the end of his life Vamshivadana Thakura settled in Bilvagrama, the village of his forefathers.19 The Bhattacharyas of Bilvagrama, so it is said, descend from him; one biography writes that there he was renowned among scholars, Bhattacharyas and pious people.

When, where and on what day Vamshivadana Thakura left this world the sources do not say; the day of his departure is not in our calendar either.

Descendants

Chaitanya Dasa had two sons — Sri Ramachandra, who was also called Ramai Thakura, and Sri Shachinandana. Ramachandra was asked for by Jahnava Mata, the shakti of Nityananda: she gave him initiation, kept him with her at Kharadaha and herself taught him Vaishnava philosophy (the journal “Gaudiya,” 22.30–37).20 So it was that Jahnava Thakurani's mercy rested on the whole line of Vamshivadananda.

Ramachandra, Vamshivadananda's grandson, found in Vraja, at Praskandana-tirtha, the Deities of Sri Rama and Sri Krishna and installed Them at Baghnapara, in the Bardhaman district; They are called Sri Rama-Kanai. Praskandana-tirtha is a ghat on the Yamuna not far from Dvadashaditya-tila. Tradition tells that when Krishna came out of the Yamuna after His struggle with Kaliya and felt cold, the twelve Adityas rose all at once to warm Him; He grew hot, and His perspiration flowed into the Yamuna — hence the name of the place: Praskandana.

Sri Ramachandra Gosvami himself was a brahmachari; the worship of Rama and Krishna at Baghnapara he entrusted to his younger brother, Shachinandana, and the sons and descendants of Sri Shachinandana Gosvami became the line of the Gosvamis of Baghnapara.

Ramachandra left a pada in which he laments that he was born only after Gauranga's departure and met none of His companions, and calls himself Vamshi's grandson:

“The Lord's dear associate is Thakura Vamshivadana: I am his son's son.” (pada of Ramachandra, 24.4)

Vamshivadana's life was described, by tradition, by his grandson Sri Vallabha Dasa in the “Vamshi-vilasa”; there are accounts of him in the “Shripata-paryatana” and the “Bhakti-ratnakara” as well, and a short biography in the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana.”21

Narahari Chakravarti, in the “Namamrita-samudra,” where his prayers call upon the Lord's associates, turns to him as well, together with Vakreshvara:

“Sri Vamshivadana, Vakreshvara, Shivananda! Dispel my sorrow and grant me bliss just once.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 33)

Significance

Vamshivadana Thakura is Krishna's flute, the eternal companion of His lips, who appeared in Navadvipa to serve Gauranga in those closest to Him. When the Lord took sannyasa, Vamshi remained as guardian of His mother and consort; when Shachi departed, he stayed with Vishnupriya as her disciple and “the exclusive vessel of her mercy.” He met Srinivasa at the Lord's house and brought him to Vishnupriya, established at her wish the service of the Deity of Gauranga, and poured out the separation of Navadvipa in a song that is sung to this day. The flute that in Vraja sang for Krishna began in Navadvipa to sing of Gauranga.

Notes

  1. He should not be confused with his namesakes: Vamshidasa Babaji (20th century); Vamshi Raya of Shrikhanda, son of Kanai Thakura and grandson of Raghunandana; Vamshivadana, son of Kanu Thakura of Bodhkhana; Vamshidasa Chakravarti, younger brother of Shyamadasa (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 10.289–296); the later padakarta Vamshidasa, a disciple of Srinivasa Acharya; Srila Gaurakishora Dasa Babaji, whose worldly name was Vamshi Dasa. “Sri Vamshivadana” is also the name of Srinivasa's Deity (“Narottama-vilasa” 11.37) and an epithet of Krishna in the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” and in Murari Gupta.
  2. One biography says that the flute “could take a human form” because all in Vraja is of spirit. We render this as the descent of an eternal associate: Krishna's flute is not a thing that became a man but a devotee full of consciousness and love; cf. the gopis' wonder at her good fortune in the “Srimad-Bhagavatam” (10.21.9).
  3. Devakinandana's line is obscure; it seems to mean that Gadadhara Dasa revealed Vamshivadana as the descent of Krishna's flute.
  4. In the biographies the names vary in spelling: Teghari, Benchiara, Bedra-para and Chine-danga; or Teghari, Venchiada, Vedadapada and Chinedanga-grama.
  5. According to one biography, Yudhishthira was not a distant descendant but Srikara's eldest son, and Srikara's sons settled in Bilvagrama, Paduli-hata and Venchiada in Kuliya.
  6. According to one biography, the youngest brother was called Krishnadasa; it gives no nicknames for the brothers.
  7. One biography converts these years as 1495 and 1506; but Chaitra of 1416 Shaka falls in the spring of 1494, and of 1427 in the spring of 1505 (78 is added to the Shaka year). Another gives “1466” — probably a corruption of “1416.”
  8. According to one biography, Vamshi was born in Madhava Dasa's house in the very days when Mahaprabhu was staying there, and Advaita Acharya was present. But the Lord stayed in Kuliya five years after His sannyasa, around 1514, when Vamshi, by either of the years given, was no longer an infant. Other biographies say only that the Lord and Advaita were present at his birth — the Lord would then have been eight or nineteen; we present this as tradition.
  9. The biographies trace the account of Devananda to the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya”; but in the ninth act of the drama Devananda is not named — he is spoken of in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” on the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” (Madhya 16). Both the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” and the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” name only the house of Madhava Dasa; that this Madhava Dasa is Chhakari, Vamshi's father, is said by the biographies. The primary sources differ also in the order of the journey: in the drama the Lord came to Kuliya from Advaita's house in Shantipur, in the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” He went from Kuliya to Shantipur.
  10. If Vamshi was born in 1505, at the Lord's sannyasa (1510) he would have been about five years old, and could have become the guardian of Shachi and Vishnupriya only later; if in 1494, about sixteen.
  11. The index of the “Pada-kalpataru” ascribes this pada to Vamshidasa, and one manuscript bears the name of Vasu Ghosha; but the signature is “Vamshi,” and scholars, like the biographies, ascribe it to Vamshivadana. The translation is ours, from the edition of the padas in our collection.
  12. When Vamshi began to serve Vishnupriya is told differently: according to some, already after the Lord's sannyasa, together with Ishana; according to others, only after Mahaprabhu's withdrawal.
  13. One biography, retelling the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” writes that Vamshivadana went to Vishnupriya and Shachimata; in the verses (4.20–24, 4.39–44) there is only Vishnupriya. And the biographies themselves say that after Shachi's departure Vamshi served Vishnupriya and Ishana; Shachi appeared to Srinivasa only in a dream (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.55). “Set him on his lap” is probably a literal reading of the words of the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (4.22), which say “embraced.”
  14. The biography cites verse 167 of the fourth chapter of the “Prema-vilasa”; in our edition the meeting is at 4.169, and further on it is Ishana who looks after Srinivasa (4.170–181), whereas in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” it is Vamshi. The primary sources differ also on where Srinivasa came from: according to the “Prema-vilasa” (4.165) and the biography, from Shrikhanda; according to the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (4.39), from Nilachala.
  15. According to one biography, he installed the Deity of Krishna — Pranavallabha — in Koladvipa only after Vishnupriya's departure.
  16. Who established the Deity of Gauranga is told differently. According to some biographies, Vamshivadana instituted His worship at Vishnupriya's wish; according to another, the Deity was installed by Vishnupriya herself (the Lord had left her His Deity), and after her departure Vamshi moved Him to Koladvipa, the present town of Navadvipa, and there instituted His service.
  17. One biography has “Phulia-Paharpur”; but it speaks at once of “the village of Kuliya,” and the “Shripata-paryatana” names Kulia-Paharpur; Phulia (Fulia), the village of Haridasa Thakura, is another place. Evidently a misprint.
  18. Both padas named are signed “Vamshivadana” and “Vamshi,” and scholars ascribe them to him; the signature “Vamshidasa” may also belong to the later poet.
  19. The biographies understand Bilvagrama differently: according to one, he moved there at the end of his life; according to another, he spent his last years there, in the village of his forefathers (from where, by tradition, Srikara had come to Kuliya); according to a third, he lived there in the summer.
  20. One biography writes that Jahnava “accepted alms” from Ramachandra; in fact she asked for the boy, as one asks for alms — she took him as her adopted son and disciple.
  21. The family biography of Vamshi is usually called the “Murali-vilasa” (by Rajavallabha); both the “Murali-vilasa” and the “Vamshi-shiksha” are late family works, and we give their accounts as tradition.
